items.desc: While human well-being depends on the health of our ecosystems, there are also countless aspects of the natural world that pose serious threats to people. items.title: Testing Einstein's laws from the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea
items.desc: Are the laws of physics truly the same everywhere in the universe? This fundamental principle, known as Lorentz invariance, lies at the heart of Einstein's theory of relativity. Yet some theories that seek to reconcile gravity with quantum physics suggest that it might not always hold. To investigate this possibility, researchers from the international KM3NeT collaboration analyzed 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events detected by KM3NeT/ORCA, a neutrino telescope located deep in the Mediterranean Sea.

items.title: Loophole listing keeps seafood qualifying as critically endangered on the menu
items.desc: One of Australia's most dangerously overfished species, redfish (Centroberyx affinis), will continue to be served on our dinner tables following its latest listing as "conservation dependent." The classification is a loophole allowing species that qualify for critically endangered listings and protections to instead be killed and sold for seafood.

items.title: Who killed British archaeologist James Starkey? Archival records shed light on an 88-year-old mystery
items.desc: Eighty-eight years after pioneering British archaeologist Starkey was shot dead while traveling from the ancient city of Lachish to Jerusalem, researchers say they have uncovered compelling new evidence explaining who was behind his murder—and why he was targeted.

items.title: Researchers develop sensors for continuous corn growth monitoring
items.desc: When is the best time to apply nitrogen? What plant response was there to fertilizer or any number of other treatments? There is a general answer to those questions now, but what if plant breeders and agronomists could download data from continuously monitored cornstalks and ears to develop specific answers for those questions?

items.title: How anxiety over climate change affects college students
items.desc: College undergraduates are anxious about climate change, with many feeling powerless and frustrated about Earth's future, yet resources to help students cope are in short supply, according to new interdisciplinary University of Utah research. The sentiment isn't limited to students studying the environment.

items.title: One in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse, study finds
items.desc: Around one in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse, according to a new study. The general-population survey of more than 7,200 adults in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia found 7% had experienced at least one form of AI-generated image-based abuse since turning 18.

items.title: Want more social media engagement? Research suggests changing the message, not your personality
items.desc: Want more engagement on social media? Stop repeating yourself. Just don't change who you are in the process. That's according to new Case Western Reserve University research suggesting that public figures can increase engagement by varying their topics and wording while "maintaining a consistent psychological voice."

items.title: Shared data ecosystem could help scientists explore new biological connections
items.desc: Scientists generate vast amounts of research data, but connecting information across studies can be difficult. The NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem is working to change that by making research data sets from 18 NIH programs easier to find, connect and analyze.

items.title: Digitalization front-runners are more vulnerable to cyberattacks
items.desc: For many business leaders, digitalization is associated with promises of greater efficiency and productivity. However, a new study by professor of accounting Jukka Sihvonen from the University of Vaasa, Finland, suggests that increasing digitalization may also raise a company's risk of falling victim to a successful cyberattack. The study has been published in the journal British Journal of Management.

items.title: Study maps Nelore cattle microbiota to reduce methane emissions
items.desc: Researchers at the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (EMBRAPA) are studying the relationship between the genetics of Nelore cattle and the microorganisms in their guts (microbiota). Nelore cattle are the most widely raised beef breed in Brazil. The goal is to develop strategies that reduce emissions of methane—a major greenhouse gas—and improve the animals' feed efficiency.

items.title: North Atlantic's 'cold blob' may contain climate nuance
items.desc: Climate observers have long tied the strength of a major ocean current to water temperatures in the so-called "cold blob" in the North Atlantic Ocean. The 965,000-square-mile (2.5 million square kilometers) area south and southeast of Greenland cooled by as much as 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit over the past century as other ocean waters warmed.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
items.desc: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

items.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
items.desc: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.

items.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
items.desc: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

items.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
items.desc: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

items.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.desc: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

items.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
items.desc: A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge.

items.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
items.desc: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

items.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

items.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
items.desc: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

items.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
items.desc: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.

items.title: NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice
items.desc: NASA satellites have captured an eerie, skull-shaped formation on a remote Antarctic island, but its haunting appearance conceals a troubling warning about melting glaciers. Unusually warm winter temperatures have exposed large areas of dark ice, potentially accelerating future melting and gradually transforming the skull's ghostly features.

items.title: IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
items.desc: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

items.title: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.

items.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
items.desc: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks.

items.title: NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past
items.desc: NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the solar system’s origins by studying 27 tiny, distant objects beyond Neptune. Scientists discovered that these ancient building blocks of planets have remained remarkably unchanged for billions of years, while their unexpected sizes and numbers challenge existing theories of planet formation.

items.title: Good Institutions Require Good People
items.desc: Well-designed laws, courts, catechisms, extrinsic motives, social approval, and even a few good and decent people are of no avail if too many people do not behave like self-respecting and other-respecting adults. Childish pride and envy, grabbing more of the sweets, Donald Trump-style, do not make for a good society.

items.title: Oligarchic World Order
items.desc: Today, some 64 heads of state or government are oligarchs, leading countries that together account for some 60% of global GDP. The question is thus no longer whether oligarchs will rule the world, but rather what kind of world they are building.

items.title: Poland’s Constitutional Civil War
items.desc: Polish right-wing populists recently stormed the country's Constitutional Tribunal, winning applause from the Kremlin and far-right fellow-travelers across Europe. As in other countries, the constitutional tribunal is the institution that distinguishes a proper democracy from a dictatorship making it a target for authoritarians.

items.title: The Tech Brotherhood Wants Sovereignty
items.desc: After centuries of nation-states, a new form of sovereignty is asserting itself. The small fraternity that controls the major digital platforms has already proven capable of even more intrusive and insidious forms of control than most states can muster.

items.title: The Far Right’s Vision for Europe
items.desc: In many ways, Europe’s far right has already won, regardless of what happens at the ballot box in the coming months. Its parties may still quarrel among themselves, but they agree on the three big issues that will define much of the European political agenda for years to come.

items.title: Europe’s Bright Future
items.desc: A narrative of European decline has taken hold, and if the EU continues on its current path, it may well materialize. But this is not a foregone conclusion: Europe retains considerable strengths on which it can build as it pursues critical reforms aimed at unleashing innovation.

items.title: A Debtors’ Club for a Fragmented World
items.desc: The newly created Borrowers’ Platform aims to facilitate knowledge-sharing and capacity-building among debtor countries, while amplifying their voices in global financial circles. But at a time when the Paris Club of sovereign creditors is increasingly unable to act collectively, the Borrowers’ Platform should ramp up its ambition.

items.title: Trump’s Tariff Fiasco Could Save Free Trade
items.desc: US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised prices and hurt businesses without reducing the trade deficit or creating manufacturing jobs. But global trade has held up better than expected, and growing public opposition to tariffs could pave the way for a retreat from protectionism.

items.title: If AI Thinks for Us, Democracy Will Suffer
items.desc: Whereas the internet buried us in information, AI enables us to outsource analysis altogether. But when it comes to grappling with humanity’s most important questions, we must resist the temptation and recognize that we all have a duty—to each other and to ourselves—to keep “showing up.”

items.desc: The removal of Bogdan Święczkowski as president of the Constitutional Tribunal has triggered a physical confrontation at the court and a political standoff between Donald Tusk’s government and the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) party. items.desc: The exponential trajectory of the latest Ebola outbreak is an urgent reminder that infectious diseases do not wait for ideal geopolitical alignments or balanced budgets.
